title: Disasters
hookLine: after earthquakes and floods, Christians give, rebuild and lament

lines: WHY DID GOD LET THIS HAPPEN?
cards: The water has gone down, and it left a line on every wall at the same height. Mud in the kitchen drawers. Photographs drying on a fence.
A church parking lot turned into a warehouse of bottled water and diapers, strangers in work gloves passing boxes hand to hand.

After a flood, an earthquake, a fire, the same question comes up on the news and at kitchen tables: why did God let this happen? The Bible doesn't give a tidy answer. But it does show what people of faith do next.

teach.b: In Luke, he himself brings up a tower that fell in Jerusalem: "Or those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem? I tell you, Nay."
The people under the tower weren't being punished for being worse than everyone else. Whatever a disaster is, the text won't let anyone point at the victims. Then there's lament.

Lamentations is a set of poems over a ruined city, and in the middle of the wreckage one line holds on: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness."

In Acts, a prophet named Agabus warns that a famine is coming, and the response is: "Then the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief unto the brethren which dwelt in Judaea."
Not a debate about why. A collection. Then rebuilding.
Nehemiah stands before the broken walls of Jerusalem and says, "Come, and let us build up the wall."

teach.h: LET US RISE UP AND BUILD.
teach.b: The people answer, "Let us rise up and build." Lament, give, rebuild. Churches today hold services of mourning after disasters, collect relief, and send crews to tear out wet drywall.
The why may never be answered. The text keeps pointing at the next morning, and the next brick.

how: After disasters, churches open their buildings as shelters and supply centers, hold services of lament, collect money through their relief agencies, and send volunteers to clean up and rebuild homes.

o: losses the Bible says should be grieved quietly and alone
floods and fires met with lament, relief and rebuilding, not blame
a word the Bible uses only for the great flood in Noah's day

p: let us rise up and build

s: Jesus says the people killed by the tower in Siloam were worse sinners
he asks if they were sinners above all others, and answers: I tell you, Nay.
"new every morning" was written over a ruined city
it's from Lamentations, poems of grief over a fallen Jerusalem.
in Acts, the disciples answer the coming famine by debating why it happens
they each send relief according to their ability.

games.q: you're one of the disciples in Antioch. a prophet named Agabus has just warned that a famine is coming, and your brothers and sisters in Judea will go hungry. what do you do?
o: wait to see if the famine really comes.
each give what you can and send relief.
argue about whether the famine is a punishment.
games.why: Acts says every man, according to his ability, determined to send relief to Judea. the answer to a coming disaster was a collection.

practice: Bring to mind one place hit recently by a flood, a storm, an earthquake or a fire, and picture one family standing in a doorway there. Hold them for a while without trying to explain anything.
If you pray, you can pray the line from Lamentations over them, that his compassions fail not; if you don't, let them stay in your thoughts a little longer.

wordCard.voice: Disasters. Floods, quakes and fires that the Bible won't blame on the victims, met with lament, with relief, and with people rising up to build.

orig.note: Hebrew: to build — the verb in Nehemiah's "let us rise up and build."

carryVoice: Your line: rebuild. In Nehemiah, the people answered, let us rise up and build. Same time tomorrow.
